newsitem.title: USA: US Democratic budget plan excludes Social Security.
newsitem.headline: US Democratic budget plan excludes Social Security.

text.p: A group of U.S. Senate Democrats on Tuesday proposed an alternative balanced budget amendment to the Constitution that would exclude Social Security trust fund surpluses.

Sen. Byron Dorgan, Democrat of North Dakota, said on the Senate floor the inclusion of growing Social Security trust funds would mask a growing deficit in other areas of government and hide a growing federal debt.
"Let's make sure the massive surpluses that will accrue in the Social Security system will be set aside," he said.
President Clinton is expected to send a letter to lawmakers stressing the danger to the Social Security system from the Republican proposal for a balanced budget amendment.

The Republican amendment, which is expected to clear the Senate Judiciary Committee this week, would require the budget be balanced each year. It includes massive Social Security surplus funds in the calculation of whether the government's funds are balanced.

This is the same method, called the "unified budget," that the White House and Congress have traditionally used to figure each year's deficit. The $107 billion budget deficit in fiscal 1996 was calculated using this method, but when Social Security and other trust funds are excluded the 1996 deficit was $174 billion.
Both Republican and Democratic proposals would change the U.S. Constitution to make it harder for Congress to raise the federal debt ceiling, to approve deficit spending, or to raise taxes.

Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch, Republican of Utah, accused the White House and Democrats of raising the Social Security issue as a way to "scare older Americans" and ultimately defeat the balanced budget amendment.
